new_entities.name: Device code flow (OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant)

quotes.text: Citizens remember Teams is not a chat room. It is an identity elevator. Therefore supervision is compulsory. If external messaging is business critical, confine it with governance. If it is not, disable it categorically.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Reframes Teams as an identity elevation path rather than a harmless chat tool.

quotes.text: This is not a breach of cryptography. It is a breach of ceremony. Device code is designed for devices without keyboards. The attacker repurposes it for social extraction.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains concisely why device code phishing works without breaking any technology.

quotes.text: Passwords can be rotated. Token's expire, but a granted permission remains until you revoke it. Therefore, revoke by default, consent by exception, and record every exception.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Gives a memorable rule for governing OAuth app consent.

quotes.text: This is not a failure of prompts. It is a failure of binding, authentication occurred. But the artifact of trust was not anchored to the device or the client.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Pinpoints why adversary-in-the-middle attacks defeat ordinary MFA.

quotes.text: Because token protection was active on managed Windows devices the stolen cookie failed off device. Continuous access evaluation cut the replayed session when sign-in risk spiked.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Names the single misconfiguration the episode identifies as nullifying MFA.

takeaways: Disable broad user consent and route all third-party app permissions through administrator consent, verified publishers and app governance.
Restrict Teams external access to an allow list and treat any chat-initiated MFA prompt or device code request as a likely attack.
Bind sessions with phishing-resistant authentication, token protection and continuous access evaluation so stolen tokens cannot be replayed.
hook: Attackers no longer need to break MFA when they can talk users into approving prompts, reading out device codes or consenting to malicious apps inside Microsoft 365. This episode walks security and identity admins through five real attack patterns in Teams, OAuth, SharePoint and token replay. You get concrete Conditional Access, consent and detection controls to close each gap.
